q: Parts of the autonomic nervous system are:
who: Divisions of the autonomic nervous system

concept.t: The autonomic nervous system (ANS) runs the body's involuntary functions. These are its two main divisions: the sympathetic and the parasympathetic.
Many books add a third, the enteric system of the gut wall.

wrong.b: Divides the whole nervous system, not the ANS.
wrong.c: Describes somatic versus autonomic control, not the parts of the ANS.
wrong.d: Not a division at all.

q: Which of the following is the correct path of a reflex arc?

concept.t: The signal enters the spinal cord by a sensory (afferent) neuron, crosses an interneuron in the grey matter and leaves by a motor (efferent) neuron to the effector.
Afferent arrives, efferent exits. The knee-jerk even skips the interneuron.

wrong.a: Ends in an afferent neuron; an arc must end in an efferent neuron to reach the effector.
wrong.b: Two afferent neurons and no way out; the arc must end in an efferent neuron.
wrong.d: Runs to the brain, but the arc closes in the spinal cord, not the brain.

q: White matter is primarily composed of

concept.t: The fat of the myelin sheath around axons makes the tissue look white.
Grey matter is made of cell bodies and unmyelinated axons.

wrong.b: Dendrites are not myelinated, so they cannot make white matter.
wrong.c: Cell bodies make up grey matter, not white.
wrong.d: Unmyelinated axons belong to grey matter; without myelin there is no white.

q: The reticular activating system (RAS), located in the brainstem, is crucial for the regulation of:

concept.t: The RAS is the ascending part of the reticular formation in the brainstem core.
It keeps the cortex awake and alert; its destruction causes coma.

wrong.a: Belongs to the cerebellum, not the RAS.
wrong.c: Belongs to the amygdala.
wrong.d: Belongs to the cerebellum.

q: Which brain structure would most likely result in death if damaged?

concept.t: The medulla oblongata holds the vital centres for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, so its damage is the most likely to kill.

wrong.a: Cerebellar damage causes ataxia, not death.
wrong.c: Reticular damage causes coma; the vital centres sit in the medulla.
wrong.d: Helps set the breathing rhythm but is not the main vital centre.

q: Which brain structure serves as the primary control center for integrating the endocrine, visceral, and autonomic nervous systems?

concept.t: The hypothalamus controls the autonomic nervous system and directs the pituitary.
So it integrates neural and hormonal control of the body for homeostasis.

wrong.a: Coordinates movement, not endocrine or autonomic control.
wrong.c: The sensory relay, not an integrator of body systems.
wrong.d: Carries out autonomic reflexes without integrating them with the endocrine system.

q: Which of the following is an inhibitory neurotransmitter?

concept.t: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter of the brain.
At GABA-A receptors it opens Cl- channels and produces IPSPs (inhibitory postsynaptic potentials).

wrong.a: Noradrenaline, a catecholamine that modulates arousal; not the standard inhibitory transmitter.
wrong.c: A catecholamine that modulates movement and reward; not the standard inhibitory transmitter.
wrong.d: Adrenaline, a catecholamine; none of these is the standard inhibitory transmitter.

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of glial cell?

concept.t: Myelin is the fatty insulation that glial cells make; it is not a cell itself.
Oligodendrocytes in the CNS, Schwann cells in the PNS.

wrong.a: True glia: the immune cells of the nervous system.
wrong.b: True glia: the star-shaped support cells of the CNS.
wrong.c: True glia: they make myelin in the CNS.

q: Which of the following is not a neurotransmitter?

concept.t: Adrenaline is the odd one out because it acts mainly as a hormone of the adrenal medulla.
Strictly it is also a catecholamine neurotransmitter, released by a few adrenergic brainstem neurons, so treat this as an odd-one-out question.

wrong.a: A classic brain monoamine transmitter.
wrong.b: A classic brain monoamine transmitter.
wrong.c: Noradrenaline, a classic brain monoamine transmitter.

q: Valium, Xanax, Rohypnol, and Halcion are:

concept.t: Valium is diazepam, Xanax alprazolam, Rohypnol flunitrazepam and Halcion triazolam: all one chemical class, the benzodiazepines.
They raise the frequency of GABA-A chloride channel opening.

wrong.b: A different class: they raise the duration of opening, not its frequency.
wrong.c: A broad functional label that also covers alcohol and barbiturates, not a chemical class.
wrong.d: A broad functional label that also covers alcohol and barbiturates, not a chemical class.

q: Which of the following substances is NOT a natural alkaloid compound?

concept.t: Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is semisynthetic, made by adding two acetyl groups to morphine.
Morphine, codeine, papaverine and thebaine occur naturally in opium, the dried sap of the poppy.

wrong.a: A natural opium alkaloid, and the starting point for heroin.
wrong.c: A natural opium alkaloid.
wrong.d: A natural opium alkaloid.

q: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia has been on antipsychotic medication for years. He presents with repetitive, involuntary, and purposeless movements of his mouth, tongue, and face, including lip-smacking and grimacing. This condition is most likely:

concept.t: Involuntary orofacial movements after months or years of neuroleptic treatment are tardive dyskinesia (tardive means late).
It is the late, often irreversible extrapyramidal effect.

wrong.a: Inner restlessness and pacing, which comes within days to weeks.
wrong.b: Muscle spasms that come within hours to days, not years.
wrong.d: Tremor, rigidity, slowness, which comes within weeks.

q: Which neuroscientific technique provides the highest temporal resolution for studying neural activity?

concept.t: EEG records the brain's electrical activity directly, so it follows changes millisecond by millisecond.
Temporal resolution is how precisely a method tracks when activity happens.

wrong.a: Depends on a blood-flow response that takes seconds.
wrong.b: Depends on tracer uptake over a minute or more.
wrong.d: A still structural image with no temporal resolution at all.

q: In Phenylketonuria (PKU), the body fails to convert phenylalanine into which substance due to a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase?

concept.t: Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine into tyrosine.
In autosomal recessive PKU the enzyme is missing, so phenylalanine accumulates and damages the brain unless a low-phenylalanine diet starts at birth.

wrong.a: A waste product of protein breakdown.
wrong.c: The precursor of serotonin.
wrong.d: The precursor of histamine.

q: A male child presents with tall stature, small testes, and learning difficulties. Karyotype analysis shows an extra X chromosome. This condition is :

concept.t: Klinefelter syndrome is an extra X in a male (47,XXY).
Tall stature, small testes, infertility and learning difficulties.

wrong.b: 45,X: a short, infertile female, with an X missing rather than extra.
wrong.c: A paternal deletion at 15q11 to q13, not an extra X.
wrong.d: Trisomy 21, not an extra X.

q: The Mach bands phenomenon is best explained by :

concept.t: Lateral inhibition means neighbouring retinal cells suppress each other.
At a light-dark border, cells on the bright side receive less inhibition from their dark neighbours and cells on the dark side receive more.
The edge is exaggerated into a brighter and a darker strip: the Mach bands.

wrong.a: Concerns dim-light versus colour vision, not edges.
wrong.b: Explains colour coding and afterimages, not brightness at an edge.
wrong.d: The adding of weak signals over time, not contrast at an edge.

q: Difficulty in seeing objects at a distance is called :

concept.t: In myopia (near-sightedness) the eyeball is too long, so distant objects focus in front of the retina and blur.
A concave lens corrects it.

wrong.b: Blurs near objects, the opposite problem.
wrong.c: Comes from an irregular cornea.
wrong.d: Blind areas caused by damage to the visual pathway, not focusing errors.

q: Which of the following areas of the brain is involved in controlling movements of the body?

concept.t: Movement is controlled by a hierarchy. Primary motor cortex (area 4, precentral gyrus) is the main cortical output.
Secondary motor cortex, the premotor cortex and supplementary motor area, programmes the patterns of movement that primary cortex executes.
No single area does the job alone.

wrong.a: The main output, but it executes patterns the secondary areas programme.
wrong.b: Programmes movement patterns but needs primary cortex to execute them.
wrong.c: Part of secondary motor cortex; it programmes movement but does not act alone.

q: In carrying out the 'fight or flight' response, the role of supervisor is assigned to the:
who: Hypothalamus, integrating endocrine and autonomic systems

concept.t: The hypothalamus integrates the endocrine and autonomic systems.
It drives both the sympathetic nervous system and the pituitary, so it supervises the whole response.

wrong.a: Carries out the hypothalamus's orders; it does not supervise.
wrong.b: Carries out the hypothalamus's orders; it does not supervise.
wrong.d: Calms the body instead, the opposite of fight or flight.

q: Which cluster of symptoms is seen in Kluver-Bucy syndrome?
who: Kluver-Bucy syndrome, anterior temporal lobe and amygdala

concept.t: Bilateral anterior temporal lobe and amygdala damage.
Psychic blindness (agnosia), hyperorality, hyperphagia and hypersexuality, with aphasia in human cases.

wrong.b: Avolition and alogia are negative symptoms of schizophrenia, and the syndrome brings hypersexuality, not asexuality.
wrong.c: The animals become placid, not hyperalert, so the last item fails.
wrong.d: Hypo-sensitivity and delayed reaction are not in the classic cluster, which centres on hyperorality and agnosia.

q: What is the term for the brain's process of regulating its own responses to stress by controlling hormone release?

concept.t: Allostasis is stability through change: the brain anticipates demands and adjusts hormone release.
Sterling and Eyer defined it in 1988.

wrong.a: Rewiring of the brain with experience, not stress regulation.
wrong.b: Cannon's stability around fixed set points, not stability through change.
wrong.d: The 24-hour cycle, not a stress response.

q: A lesion of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) produces:
who: Hetherington and Ranson, VMH satiety centre (1940)

concept.t: The VMH was the classic satiety centre (Hetherington and Ranson, 1940).
Destroy the satiety centre and the animal keeps eating: hyperphagia and obesity.

wrong.a: Circadian rhythms depend on the suprachiasmatic nucleus, not the VMH.
wrong.b: Follows lateral hypothalamic lesions (Anand and Brobeck, 1951), not VMH lesions.
wrong.c: Follows failure of ADH from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei.

q: Which gland regulates the circadian rhythm in the human beings?

concept.t: The question asks for a gland, and the pineal gland turns the clock's signal into night-time melatonin.
The clock itself is the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.

wrong.a: Holds the clock itself (the suprachiasmatic nucleus), but the question asks for a gland.
wrong.b: Coordinates movement; it keeps no clock.
wrong.c: The master gland of other hormones; it keeps no clock.

q: Masters and Johnson's sexual response cycle is distinct from Kaplan's model. Which of the following correctly reflects Masters and Johnson's sequence?

concept.t: Masters and Johnson (1966) described four phases: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution.
Men have a refractory period after orgasm, but it is not a separate phase of the cycle.

wrong.b: No model starts with plateau.
wrong.c: Mixes in desire from Kaplan and swaps resolution for the male refractory period.
wrong.d: Putting desire first is Helen Singer Kaplan's (1979) change, not Masters and Johnson's.

q: A person suffered a head injury in a road accident several years ago. Since the accident, he is unable to form new memories. He can remember many things which he did before the accident, but he cannot remember what he said ten minutes ago. The part of the brain which is most probably injured is:

concept.t: Failing to form new memories while old ones survive is anterograde amnesia.
It is the signature of hippocampal damage, as in the patients H.M. and R.B.

wrong.a: Serves vital functions; it does not consolidate memory.
wrong.c: Carries reflexes and sensorimotor signals; it does not consolidate memory.
wrong.d: Serves arousal; it does not consolidate memory.

q: According to Karl Lashley's research on memory storage, where did he conclude that memories are primarily stored in the brain?
who: Karl Lashley, mass action and equipotentiality

concept.t: No cortical lesion erased a maze habit in Lashley's rats; he found no localised engram.
The deficit depended on how much cortex was removed (mass action), not where (equipotentiality).

wrong.a: The opposite of his result: he found no localised engram.
wrong.c: The hippocampus's role in forming memories emerged only later, with H.M.
wrong.d: The deficit depended on how much cortex was removed, not which lobes.

q: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results in:

concept.t: Thiamine deficiency first causes Wernicke's encephalopathy: confusion with lapses of attention, ataxia (loss of muscle coordination) and ophthalmoplegia with nystagmus.
Survivors develop the amnesia of Korsakoff's syndrome.
So the combined syndrome affects attention and coordination as well as memory.

wrong.a: True (confusion with lapses of attention), but only half the picture.
wrong.b: True (ataxia), but only half the picture.
wrong.d: Fails because a and b are both features of the syndrome.

q: The left hemisphere is:

concept.t: The left hemisphere is dominant for language in about 95 percent of right-handers and most left-handers.
So it was called the major or dominant hemisphere.

wrong.a: A right-hemisphere strength.
wrong.b: The old label for the right hemisphere.
wrong.d: A right-hemisphere strength.

q: Cutting through a person's corpus callosum causes the person to:

concept.t: Corpus callosotomy is surgery for intractable epilepsy.
The hemispheres cannot share information, which shows up in tasks needing both.

wrong.a: Patients stay alive after the surgery.
wrong.b: Patients stay sighted.
wrong.c: Patients can still speak, because the left hemisphere still speaks.

q: Ria has difficulty enunciating words correctly and speaks in a slow and laboured way; her speech often makes sense, but it includes only keywords. Which part of her brain is damaged?

concept.t: Slow, effortful, telegraphic speech that still makes sense is Broca's (non-fluent) aphasia.

wrong.a: Damage here gives fluent, empty speech with poor comprehension, the opposite pattern.
wrong.c: Damage here gives fluent, empty speech with poor comprehension.
wrong.d: True but too broad; Broca's area is the specific answer.

q: Prosopagnosia results in an inability to :

concept.t: Prosopagnosia is a visual agnosia for faces after fusiform gyrus damage.
The source key gives (b), which is wrong.

wrong.b: Loss of taste is ageusia; the source key's choice here is an error.
wrong.c: A motor sign, like the masked face of Parkinson's disease.
wrong.d: Failure to recognise objects is object agnosia, not the face-specific form.

q: A patient presents with an inability to perform coordinated, purposeful movements, despite having intact motor function, sensation, and comprehension of the task. When asked to brush their hair, they cannot sequence the movements. This deficit is best described as:

concept.t: Apraxia is loss of learned purposeful movement with strength, sensation, coordination and comprehension intact.
It is ideational apraxia: the steps cannot be sequenced.

wrong.a: A failure of recognition, not of movement.
wrong.b: Cerebellar incoordination, but coordination is intact here.
wrong.d: Loss of reading.

q: Which of the following neurological conditions is NOT classified as a neurodegenerative disorder?

concept.t: Epilepsy is recurrent seizures from synchronous neural discharge.
It is an episodic disorder with normal function between attacks, not a progressive loss of neurons.

wrong.a: Neurodegenerative: progressive loss of substantia nigra dopamine neurons.
wrong.b: Neurodegenerative: progressive loss of cortical and hippocampal neurons.
wrong.d: Neurodegenerative: progressive loss of striatal GABA neurons.
